utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to the technical booth, the interpreters, the legal assistants, the registrar, the office of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused. As we promised yesterday, we're going to render our decision regarding the motion of the Prosecution to admit into evidence the statement of the witness Tariq Malik. I'm going to read slowly for the benefit of the interpreters. On the 29th of September, 2000, the Prosecutor filed a motion for the Chamber to admit the statement of witness Tariq Malik. In her motion, the Prosecutor underlined that this statement should be evaluated in the context of the statement of the witnesses, of the expert witnesses, White, Clark, Brown, Klonowski, and Alonso. The Prosecutor indicates that, for this reason, its motion is based on Rule 94 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, recognising that the statement of Mr. Malik does not fully fit within the context of the provisions of that rule. The Prosecutor finally specified that the Defence counsel were contacted and that they have no objection to the admission of that statement. At the hearing yesterday, the Defence first indicated that they were, indeed, in agreement. However, when the Chamber started to render its decision, the Defence interrupted the Chamber and notified the Chamber that in fact they objected to the admission if the witness is expected to appear. The Chamber would like to make a few observations. By way of introduction, the Chamber would like to note that the Prosecutor did not file her motion simultaneously in both official languages. I'm talking about the motion itself and not of the statement and the annexes. This is a very brief document. In the interest of expediency, the Chamber is nevertheless going to rule. On the substance, the statement that the Prosecutor is requesting admission of is neither dated nor signed. The witness also did not initial the pages of the text. It would therefore be appropriate for the Prosecutor to have the statement authenticated by the witness during the witness's appearance in court. If the witness for one reason or another does not appear, it would be up to the Prosecution to file with the registrar an initialled, dated, and signed statement. This new document would replace the previous statement. In any event, the statement of Mr. Malik constitutes a relevant piece of evidence, and the Chamber needs to verify that it has probative value. It therefore can be admitted, in conformity with Rule 89 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, once Mr. Malik appears and can be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: That is the decision of the Chamber. Mr. Prosecutor, now I think we can now call to the witness box the witness to continue her testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness U. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. I hope you feel rested today. I wish to remind you that you are still testifying under oath, and you will be answering questions that Mr. Saxon is going to put to you. Will you please get close to the microphone, if you can, and make yourself as comfortable as possible. Mr. Saxon, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Witness U, yesterday you described how Mladjo Radic came to your sleeping room at the Omarska camp and called out Jadranka Cigelj several times. Would this occur during the evening or during the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Witness U, were you ever called out at night from that sleeping room?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear anything, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: How often were you called out at night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several times.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: But I'm afraid we cannot hear. The microphone is not working.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're told the microphone is not working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There appears to be a problem, Witness U. We cannot hear you. Let us see if we can fix it. I think we're waiting for someone to come into the courtroom to try and fix the microphone, as it doesn't appear to be working. Witness U, I am not going to say 1, 2, 3, but can you hear me? We're just trying to test the microphone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it working now or not? The interpreters are hearing, so I think we can try and continue, Mr. Saxon. Excuse us, Witness, for this technical problem, but we're going to try and continue. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Witness U, do you know the identity of the person who called you out at night?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We're very sorry, but the microphone of the witness is not working. I'm sorry. Yes. Yes, it's all right now. Could the witness be asked to repeat her answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. The interpreters are telling us that they can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: But they can now, Your Honour. The interpreters can hear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we have already, at the same time, the indication that it's working. So let's continue, Mr. Saxon. We're not accustomed to these interruptions, but we can't help it. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will repeat my last question.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Witness U, do you know the identity of the person who called you out at night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: When you were called out at night, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a room along the corridor, at the end of the corridor. There was a room there, and I was taken to that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if I could ask you to please take the exhibit that was marked yesterday as Prosecution 3/150 and place that back on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Witness U, can you pick up the pointer and indicate on that diagram next to you where you were taken at night.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would go out of the room, walk along the corridor, and at the end, this room here.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: And what is the number on that diagram of that room that you're pointing to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is room B1. I think it was that room.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Could you pick up a pen that is next to you and write the letter "U" in that room where you were taken.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Witness U, what was in that room on the nights --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Witness U, what was in that room on the nights when you were taken there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guard who would take me there would take me to that room because it was dark, of course, and I could feel that there were mattresses on the ground. He would rape me. Then I would stay behind in the room. He would leave, and then all the time, one after another, others would come in -- I don't know the exact number -- but, unfortunately, I don't know who they were, and they also raped me.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Witness U, were you ever taken out during the day at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: How many times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Where were you sitting when you were called on these two occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: And where were you taken on those two occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the same room.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Is that the room that you marked as B1 on that diagram?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: What happened when you were taken to that room during the day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same man did it. He took me out. He took me to that room. First he raped me, and then afterwards again others entered, I don't know exactly, three or four men who raped me. But, unfortunately, I don't know those men. I never saw them in my life. But as it was daytime, I may be able to recognise them.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I'm having problems with my headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if that diagram could be removed now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Witness U, when you say these men raped you at Omarska, do you mean that they penetrated you with their penis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Did you experience bleeding due to the multiple rapes that you endured at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, throughout I was there.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Were you ever provided with any sanitary supplies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Did you ever ask for any sanitary supplies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply I knew where I was, and it never occurred to me to address anyone and seek his assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: What did you do to cope with this bleeding?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It was so shocking that perhaps I borrowed from some women who had vests -- or who borrowed their underwear -- lent me their underwear. Sometimes I would put paper. Anyway, that is how I coped.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Witness U, I'd like to ask you to turn your attention to call-outs of other persons at Omarska. Are you familiar with an area in the restaurant building at the Omarska camp that was known as the "glass house"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: When, if ever, were prisoners called out of the "glass house"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This could have been at the end of July.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Where were you when the prisoners were called out of the "glass house"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the prisoners who were called out of the "glass house" that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Who did you recognise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Begic.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: How did you know Dr. Begic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Dr. Begic from before. He was a physician.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: What was Dr. Begic's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say with certainty whether he was a Muslim or a Croat. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Who else did you recognise as they were called out of the "glass house" that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day, Dr. Kosuran was also called out, whom I knew. That is what I can remember regarding the "glass house."

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Were there any teachers called out that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. My teacher, Crnkic, a mathematics teacher who was also in the "glass house."

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Do you know the ethnicity of Professor Crnkic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Were any relatives of yours called out that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Could you see where these prisoners were taken at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Where were they taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taken out of the "glass house" and then led around the building to the "red house" which was at the end of the pista, as we called it, or at the edge of the compound.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: What happened that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: That night, in my opinion, the people who were called out were most probably executed. The whole night we could hear gunfire. I repeat, we listened to the gunfire and the noise made by the guards who were cursing, and I quote, they were cursing "Ustashas," "balijas," and that's all.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Witness U, the next morning, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next morning, when the detainees came to the restaurant to eat, it was terrible. There were quite a number of our friends -- my friends and acquaintances did not come to the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Did you see any trucks the next morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Early, before dawn, one of the women, I wouldn't like to name her now, went to the toilet which was across the way from our room. This toilet had a window, and she saw trucks with corpses, so that two other colleagues and myself went there. That was the only time that I went there to look, and it was true, there were trucks there with corpses.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Can you describe these trucks that you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see, since these were only seconds of time that we had, that these trucks were like dumpers, that is what we called these trucks, which were used to transport ore in the mine. So my opinion is that they were that kind of truck.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Did you ever see the men who were called out from the "glass house" again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: You mentioned previously that there were quite a number of your friends and acquaintances who did not come to the restaurant the next morning. Did those friends and acquaintances ever come to the restaurant again while you were detained at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Witness U, prior to the armed conflict in 1992, did you know a man named Mr. Suljic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: How did you know Mr. Suljic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted), and I knew him extremely well, both him and his parents.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: What was Mr. Suljic's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that his father was Muslim and his mother was Serb, so I don't know what to tell you in answer to your question. I think he was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Suljic at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only on that occasion when I saw his tragic end in the camp.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: What happened to Mr. Suljic when you saw him at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Suljic -- that is to say, a group of guards, some were in the middle of the pista, hit Mr. Suljic with various objects. As far as I was able to see, they beat him to death.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: And where were you at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Approximately how far from Mr. Suljic were you at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm able to judge, from where I was to where he was, it might have been ten to 15 metres. That is my assessment.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Suljic after that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: When you saw Mr. Suljic being beaten on that occasion, was it daytime or nighttime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Daytime.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Witness U, previously you described how you were transferred to the Trnopolje camp on the 3rd of August, 1992. When, if ever, did you see Zoran Zigic at the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that same day. On the 3rd of August.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: About what time of day did you see Mr. Zigic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was around noon or perhaps in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Where inside the Trnopolje camp were you when you first saw Zoran Zigic that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the school building in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: And where was Zoran Zigic when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were inside, and we could see through the window. We could see him arrive, Mr. Zigic arrive, and as far as I remember, there were two or three other men with him.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: When you say "we," that "we could see him arrive," who was with you at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: The women who were detained in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: How was Zoran Zigic dressed that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day too Zoran was wearing a military uniform with a red beret, a cap. The description is the same as I gave yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: What happened, if anything, as Zoran Zigic approached the entrance to the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoran Zigic went into the courtyard, and while he was entering the courtyard, the guard who was at the entrance in front of our room ordered us women to lie down on the floor, and he said, "Lie down. Zoran Zigic is coming."

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Did you lie down on the floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: And as you lay down on the floor, what, if anything, could you hear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zigic addressed the guard who was standing at the door and asked him where the women were.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: What else, if anything, did Mr. Zigic say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He repeated the question. He said, "Where are the women?" So that the guard standing at the doorway told him that there were no women there. I think that was an order when he said to him, "I'm responsible here for these people. So please, Mr. Zigic, would you leave this area."

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: And during that time, were you able to recognise the voice of Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Zigic say anything about work or a job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His words afterwards were the following: "I'm going to Omarska now. I have to finish off a job there."

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Witness U --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Witness U, following your detention in 1992, what efforts did you make to learn the fate of your husband?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, as -- I know 100 per cent the end my husband came to, and I registered this with the International Red Cross. I registered his name and surname as somebody who had disappeared, and I'm waiting for their answer.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Very briefly, what did you learn about your husband's end?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: From more than a hundred witnesses, and even that is a conservative number, later on when I went (redacted), they told me that my husband was beaten up, that my husband was killed in the Omarska camp in broad daylight, and there were a hundred witnesses to this.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Witness U --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hundreds of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: -- after you were released from detention, did you and your children eventually leave Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Who lives in your apartment in Prijedor today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Serbian family.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: How would you describe the impact of losing your husband and your own experiences in the camps on your life today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that in 1992, my life stopped. First of all, I don't feel like a woman anymore. There's no more happiness in our home. We don't experience any nice moments any more, any good days. We don't know when our birthdays are anymore. We're living. Sometimes I say I'm just living. I have two children, and I have to live for them.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Witness U, are you able to continue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Can you describe how Zoran Zigic looked when you saw him in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that, from the aspects of a woman, Zoran Zigic was a very, very handsome man and that he looked excellent in the uniform he wore in 1992. That's my answer.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: About how tall was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only tell you roughly and say that he was tall. Perhaps 188, 1 metre 88. That's my assessment. He was slim, he had a dark complexion, and let me repeat, he was very handsome.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: How would you describe Mr. Zigic's hair?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had black hair.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: About how old would you say Mr. Zigic was in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say he was the same age as my husband. Perhaps not exactly. One or two years difference. But he was about 38 years old, possibly 40.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Have you seen Zoran Zigic since you left the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the television screen about two years ago.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Witness, let me rephrase that last question. Have you seen Zoran Zigic since you left the Omarska and Trnopolje camps? Would your answer be the same?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Since you saw Zoran Zigic in the Trnopolje camp, have you seen him on television?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: And approximately when was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: About two years ago.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Witness U, although eight years have passed since your confinement in the Keraterm, Omarska, and Trnopolje camps, do you think that you could identify the person you knew as Zoran Zigic today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can try.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: Would you please look around the courtroom to determine if you could identify the person whom you referred to in your testimony as Zoran Zigic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zigic is sitting in the first row. He is wearing a white shirt, a tie, a pink or violet one, bluish, and a jacket. I can't say if it's blue or black, but it's dark blue or black, anyway.

utterances.speaker: THE DEFENCE
utterances.text: When you say that Mr. Zigic is sitting in the first row, is that the row closest to the wall or the row away from the wall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Further away from the wall. In the first row closest to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the record could reflect a positive identification of the accused Zigic. Your Honour, at this time I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Krstan Simic, what is the order for the cross-examination, please? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I shall be putting questions to the witness; Mr. Jovanovic, and Mr. Stojanovic, and it will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment, please. I'm going to consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness U, do you feel tired? Would you like to have a rest, or do you feel up to continuing until approximately 11.00?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Mr. Simic, Mr. Krstan Simic has the floor. Witness, you are now going to be answering questions put to you by the Defence counsels. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please go ahead. Your witness, Mr. Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness U, first of all, I'd like to express my sincere condolences for everything you have gone through.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about the time you spent in Omarska. I hope that they won't be as painful as the things you've had to talk about over the last few minutes. You said that when you arrived in Omarska, you were put up in the "white house," that you spent several hours there, and you described that place. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: You also testified that at one point a group of soldiers, guards or something like that, moved towards that place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Can you tell us or do you happen to know whether they were soldiers, members of the security system, or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't answer that question. I think they were both of them, both types. But as I had never seen any of those men, I can't tell you their names or what kind of uniforms they were all wearing, but I think they were military uniforms and police uniforms as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you. You also testified that a member of the Security Service issued an order and said, "Don't go up to those women."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Could you identify that individual, the member of the Security Service, perhaps his name or uniform, if you happen to know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know the person, but I can state that that particular individual was wearing a police uniform. I would be happy if I were able to tell the Court his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Witness U, my last question: Those persons obeyed the order of that individual and did not disturb you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. K
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. And once again, I am very sorry for everything that you have experienced.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Krstan Simic. Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness U, good morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Jovanovic. I'm an attorney from Belgrade and, together with lawyer Toma Fila, we represent the defence of the accused Mr. Mladjo Krkan. Like my colleague before me, I, too, should like to say how sorry I am for everything that you have had to go through, all your sufferings.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will be brief. I just need some information. You stated that with Mrs. Zlata Bilajac, you were in the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: And that you were put up in a room at the end of the corridor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, between that room and the corridor, was there any kind of partition, a partition wall or door or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any door. I know that I passed by, and in the room there was a bench next to the window, and the two of us sat on that bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: How large was the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: The room was a narrow one but a long one, as far as I was able to assess. The length -- the room ran the entire length of the "white house," I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about those unfortunate events and said that twice -- you were taken out twice during the day from the restaurant and taken to the large room on the first floor at the end of the corridor in that building. Can you describe the situation? There were the stairs, the staircase leading from the restaurant to the first floor, and the corridor. Were there any guards there, any investigators, interrogators? Did you hear anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: And one more question: Were there any guards in the corridor at night in front of the rooms where you slept, where the women slept, either outside or in the immediate vicinity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Never?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Jovanovic. I think that it's Mr. Stojanovic's turn now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I have to say "Witness." It's in your interest that I don't say any names. My name is Slobodan Stojanovic, from Belgrade, and Mr. Simo Tosic, an attorney from Banja Luka, is with me here, and together we represent the Defence of Mr. Zoran Zigic. We know that you have had to experience terrible suffering in these camps, and I am truly and sincerely sorry for that, and we'll try and keep our questions brief. I should like to help you to clarify -- I should like you to help us clarify certain points. Before this, you had some talks with the representatives of the OTP, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, in one of your conversations, say that Zigic was a family friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I add something to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to burden you with any lengthy answers, but if you are brief.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The event in Keraterm when you saw your late husband and Zigic, you said that this was at the end of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you help us and be more specific perhaps? I don't suppose you remember the exact date, but was it toward the end, the last week; a little more specific?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon, were you going to make an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting, Mr. Stojanovic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked the witness to help us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do wish to help, and everything that I say here is the truth and nothing but truth. As far as I recall, it could have been the end of June, perhaps the beginning of July. It was either the 1st or 2nd of July or the end of June, but quite definitely it was that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I now have just a few more questions with respect to the event that took place in Trnopolje. If I'm correct, you said that Zigic came looking for women. Which women? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: The women who had arrived from Omarska that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We heard that you were together with those women in Omarska. Did you happen to notice, during their stay in Omarska, whether Zigic was in any contact -- had any contacts with those women in any way whatsoever? Did he try to approach the women?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about Omarska.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Omarska, and my answer is No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more clarification, please. The Prosecution, in summary of their conversation with you, noted that you did not see Zigic in Trnopolje, and I'm going to read out the sentence. It's not your statement, it is a proffer by the Prosecution about the talk with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And it is, for our colleagues of the Prosecution, the last sentence in the proffer. "The witness did not see Zigic, but she heard his voice and she heard the guard addressing that person by the name of Zigic."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So we got that information from the Prosecution, not from you. We had a different answer today, that you saw Zigic, in fact. Could you tell us something to clarify that dilemma?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are no problems there. There was probably a misunderstanding. We were in the room with windows, and as you approach Trnopolje from the road, we were able to see on the road -- I was able to and the other women -- to see him approach. He was already there. And the guard said, at that moment, "Zigic is coming." So it happened simultaneously, at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness U, I should like to extend our gratitude once again to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'd like to thank Their Honours as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Stojanovic. I think no other Defence counsel wish to cross-examine, according to what Mr. Krstan Simic told us. So, Mr. Saxon, do you have any re-examination for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Witness U, you told counsel for the Defence that on the two occasions when you were taken out during the day and taken to the first floor of the restaurant building, that you said that you saw no guards there or interrogators. What time of day was that? In other words, what was going on during that period of day when you were called out on those two occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I answered exactly. The question was when I was taken there did I meet anyone. At night, no. A man led me. I don't know who he was. As it was nighttime, I didn't come across anyone. The men who later entered my room and who raped me, I couldn't see them or recognise them, unfortunately. Also, on two occasions when I was taken out during the daytime, my answer was that, on that occasion, I didn't meet anyone. I didn't come across anyone, meet anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And on those two occasions when you were taken out during the daytime, what was going on in the restaurant at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was during lunchtime, when the detainees came to have lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And would the guards and interrogators also have lunch?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon. Judge Fouad Riad, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'd just like to put some of your testimony in perspective, and I'll be very brief not to increase the strain in which you are definitely. Going back to what you said yesterday, I think you said that Zigic took your husband by the arm to the entrance and told you, "Take a good look at your husband. He will fall first for the freedom of this town." What did you understand from that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went back home, I was very upset. All of us here in this courtroom will each have their own interpretation of this statement, but the way I understood it was that my husband would disappear. Unfortunately, that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did he do that in a defiant way, in a threatening way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. It seemed like a normal conversation. Of course, a provocative one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, I'll just try to go further with the same. You said that when you were -- apparently when he came, I think, to Trnopolje, you heard him say, "I'm going to Omarska to finish a job." Was that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: He did not mention what job it was. Nobody ever told you what happened that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: When you went to, when you went (redacted), you said -- I'm sorry, wherever you went, you heard from witnesses that your husband was killed on Omarska in broad daylight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And did they tell you approximately which date it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have never managed to find out the exact date, but it could have been a day or two before I was picked up to be taken to the camp. That is the information I have. It could have been the 11th or the 12th or the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And do you remember approximately which date it was when Zigic came to Trnopolje to say he's going to a mission in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The 3rd of August. With regard to this incident when he came to Trnopolje to ask about women and the guard then told him, "This is my responsibility, this is my territory," did you understand what it was about, why he was coming and what the guard then was defending?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say what is accurate. Zigic didn't do anything. He didn't try to do anything, and he went away quickly. I have no right to say now or to think what he had in mind when he said that, nor what his intention was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Again, concerning the witnesses who told you about your husband's death, did they more or less tell you who was present at that day, the guards or the camp leaders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a wide range of disparate information so that really here in this Tribunal, I wouldn't like, nor have I the right, to give names of people who were there because I myself did not witness it. But I do know with certainty that my husband is no longer alive, and I think that 100 per cent the gentlemen sitting here, they all know my husband well. They know his first and last name, and they know when he was killed and why. I am sure of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you don't know anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Still concerning the killing, you mentioned that prisoners were taken out of the "glass house"; you saw that from the toilet window, and I want to repeat what you said about the shooting and seeing the trucks collecting them. Since you were very present, do you remember who was the leader of the camp at that time or the guards around among those you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Then I just ask you a question, a small one, before going to a difficult one. You said that Mr. Prcac came with a list of women the last day, and you were among this list. Is this the only time you saw him, the only time he was present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps on one more occasion that I saw him in the corridor in front of our room. That is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Does that mean that he was not often there, or it was you -- you're not always accessible to see people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't see people because I was a specific case in that camp. I was a person who just sat there quietly in silence so that I couldn't see much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that the women told you that Krkan was a shift leader. Did you see him often around, at night or by day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw Krkan often at night, probably when he or when his duty -- his shift was on duty, and I said yesterday how I saw him and where. That is the truth. So in our room when he would bring us food, and when he would appear at the door to call out Jadranka Cigelj to come out or to come and see him for a while, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: All right. If your memory can serve you, the man who used to -- the guard that came to you several times at night to take you to this unfortunate room, was it during the shift of Krkan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It was not? It was never in the shift of Krkan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Do you know whose shift it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I have to thank you for the very precise testimony you gave and being so fair and not trying to say anything you don't know. Please know that, through this Tribunal, the whole world is sharing your grief, and I wish you courage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Madam Judge Wald. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Witness U, I have only two questions. One, when you arrived at Omarska, is it true that you never saw your husband? He was no longer there when you got to Omarska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Did you ask people at that time around the camp where he was or whether he was still there? You mentioned that you heard later on in a different place from a lot of witnesses, but at the time, did you ask people at Omarska where he was or if something had happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did ask because, throughout my stay there, I was waiting for him to appear. But everyone knew, including the women and the men with whom I was able to have any contact, and this was very rare. The women I was with, they knew, but they probably hid it from me so that I would survive more easily. So they concealed it from me. They would say, he's in hospital in Banja Luka, or he's here or there, so that throughout that time I lived in expectation that he would appear. And it was only on that day, the 3rd of August, when I left the camp and when I was in Trnopolje, a friend of ours managed to have the strength to tell me, "(redacted) has been killed. You must accept that and not wait for him anymore."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. I'm sorry to go over such sad details. My last question is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm sorry to put you through that again. One last question, which is an ordinary one. When in the beginning the group of soldiers or -- came towards you and then another guard came along and said, "Don't approach those women," was there any indication that you could tell at the time that the guard that protected you by saying, "Don't approach those women," was just an ordinary guard of rank, the same as other guards or soldiers in the camp, or whether he held some higher position of authority, like a shift leader or an official in the camp? Did he appear to be just another guard telling the other guards, "Don't come near these women," or did he appear to be somebody of a higher rank or position? Could you tell? If you couldn't, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was an ordinary guard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Witness U, I have a few small questions for you which will not take too long. You mentioned the incident in the "white house," and you said that there were people in military uniform and the police. How do you make a distinction between military uniforms and police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a military uniform was grey in colour, greyish-green, and a police uniform consisted of a light blue shirt and blue trousers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you see those military men and those policemen later on in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell us what were their duties in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those guards mistreated people, beat them during lunch, at the pista. I'm saying what I saw. That was the work they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness U, when you say "those guards," you're referring to the guards wearing military uniforms and police uniforms that you saw before in the "white house"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm referring to both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could you tell us how many different uniforms there were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know and as far as I was able to see, there was the police uniform and the military uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were there both at the same time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS U [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Witness U, I have no more questions for you. You have answered our questions, many questions, put to you by the Prosecution, the Defence, the Judges, with a great deal of courage. Is there something that you would like to say and that you have not been asked? Is there something that you would like to tell us in addition to what you have already said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to address myself to this Trial Chamber, the gentlemen in the Defence counsel, the gentlemen who are on trial, and to say that I think this testimony of mine was so brief and concise but one from which it is possible to infer the conclusion as to what I lived through where I was. My suffering still continues. Probably my suffering will never come to an end. I have lost the man who meant a great deal for me, who was a good husband, a good father. We miss him so. We need him. But please let me say one more thing. I arrived at Omarska. I didn't know why, because we were never part of any kind of organisation. We did not engage in politics. We were honest, honourable citizens of our town Prijedor. We never made any distinction between people on the basis of ethnicity, be they Serbs, Croats, or Muslims. They were all the same. We loved people. We socialised with them. And when I arrived at the Omarska camp and went in for interrogation, I learnt there my interrogator was Drago Meakic, the gentleman who was quite -- who treated me decently. My charges were, "(redacted), it says here," and I read it out, because Comrade Meakic knew me, and it said there, "(redacted), you gossiped about the Serb army. You criticised the Serb army." I appeal to you as human beings, what kind of an accusation is that? What were the accusations against my husband so that he no longer lives and my life is at a standstill? That is all I have to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too, Witness U. You were expelled from life, as many other people, as you said, but we hope that you will find good reasons to continue to live a full life. And as you said, there are no differences between people, and I think we must think once again over this issue of being a Muslim or a Croat or a Serb is not a defect. It's not a fault. It contributes to the diversity and beauty of the world. Imagine what kind of a world it would be if we would all be the same. That would be monotonous. But if we have differences among which we can establish harmony, then the world will be a beautiful place. So you have this ideal and this way of thought, and that in itself is a good reason to continue living in spite of the terrible circumstances, your personal circumstances, and we hope that you will have ahead of you some good and happy days. So thank you, Witness, for coming here. We wish you a safe journey back to your place of residence, and I will ask the usher to accompany you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now we're going to have a half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: She spoke her name, the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Saxon. I know you have some exhibits to tender, so please proceed. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. At this time the Prosecution would move for the admission of the Prosecution's Exhibits 3/148 to 3/151.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Krstan Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're talking on behalf of all Defence counsel? MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So the documents listed by the Prosecutor will be admitted into evidence. So let us now have a half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Yes, Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour. The Prosecution would call Witness Nihad Haskic. This witness has been granted protective measures with regard to only facial distortion. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day to you, Mr. Haskic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're now going to read the solemn declaration that the usher is going to hand to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Try and sit comfortably. Perhaps you need to adjust your headsets. Thank you for coming. You are now going to be answering questions put to you by the Prosecutor, Mr. Waidyaratne, and afterwards you'll be answering questions from the Defence and the Judges, but first of all it is Mr. Waidyaratne. Mr. Waidyaratne, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Could you state your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Haskic, Nihad.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What is your date of birth and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: The 25th of August, 1958, Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you born in the Prijedor town?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Where did you reside in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: In 1992, I resided in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Which part of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: It's called Zagrad. Murharem Suljanovic, number 50, is the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you married in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you have children?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: One child, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How old was she?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Eleven.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you employed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What was your employment? Could you describe as to what you did in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: I worked on a construction site with telephonics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you have any other business?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before that I had a cevapcici kiosk.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, in April 1992, did you have your wife and child with you at the place of residence, at your place of residence?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: In May, did your wife and child go to any other place?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they went to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Why did they leave you?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Well, they went allegedly sort of for a holiday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did they come back after that in the month of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: They have not returned to the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Why didn't they come back in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Because the conditions weren't right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Could you describe more as to these conditions that you speak of?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: They couldn't return because on the 30th of April, the power was taken over and everything became topsy-turvy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now you said on the 30th of April, power was taken. Can you describe as to exactly what you mean by this?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Up until then, there were one set of authorities and, on the night of the 30th, there was a takeover of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: The Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, did you go to work after the 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Because everything was stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Could you describe more as to what this everything -- what you meant by "everything was stopped" and by whom?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't. I worked for the last day in Rasavci, and when I went to the post office on Friday to work, they said that there would be no work until further notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Who said this, that there would be no work?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: The supervisory organs in the post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know which ethnicity or which ethnic group these people belonged to?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: These people who -- the supervisory organs that you spoke of.

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: They were Serb Orthodox.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, what was your ethnicity? What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: I'm a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You mentioned that the power was taken in Prijedor and that it was by the Serbs. Could you say as to what you observed on the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: In the morning, there were lots of policemen and soldiers. There were checkpoints everywhere and all movement was practically made impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: You could feel fear of all those soldiers and policemen in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know who these policemen and these soldiers who were in town, to which ethnic group they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: I didn't know, but I assumed that they were all of the Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I would draw your attention to the 24th of May, 1992. Were you aware that, during this time, Kozarac was attacked?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: In town from the refugees, the people fleeing Kozarac. I met them in town, and the people said that Kozarac was burning and had been attacked and that they were running away to save their lives, mostly towards Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Who were these refugees or the people that were fleeing? What ethnic group did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you learn from them as to whether the surrounding villages or the areas of Kozarac, whether these villages were attacked?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What are the areas or the villages that you got to know that were attacked?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Brdjani, Softici, Kamicani, Kozarusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: During this time, were you at home in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you observe as to what happened in the surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Around Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. And even in Kozarac and the other surrounding areas.

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: On the hill too. You could see that the hill of Hambarine-Carakovo was also attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see any houses or any property being damaged?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: You mean in Prijedor or in the surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: In the areas of Kozarac and Hambarine and the surrounding areas.

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: As Kozarac is far off, I couldn't see, but you could see Hambarine. You could see the hill from Prijedor, and you could see the houses burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, on the 30th of May, 1992, were you in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Where were you?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: I was in my part of town, in my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Could you describe what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: That day, in the morning, that part of the old town was attacked, Zagrad, on Saturday morning, in the early-morning hours. The army -- there was a proclamation that white flags should be hung out and that we should surrender. The army came up. The soldiers made everybody get out of their houses, and they put us in a bus by the high-rise building and took us off to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you said that the army came. Did you see any of these armed personnel who came into the part of your town?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: They were soldiers in camouflage uniforms. I didn't know them. I can't say that I know them when I don't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: With respect to you, when you were in the house, what did you do? What were you ordered to do?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: I was ordered to put a white flag out on my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And thereafter, what did you do? Did you get onto the street?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: We all went out into the street, and we moved spontaneously towards the high-rise building, towards town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, when you got down to the street, did you see any other persons, your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw my neighbour Fuad Nekinovic [sic], who was lying there dead in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You mentioned the name Fuad. Is it Nekinovic or Ekinovic?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Ekinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Well, he was killed. He was lying in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Who were the other people who were on the street and who were taken towards the skyscraper?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: They were all my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: To which ethnic group, if you know, did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: They were all of the Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You said that you were taken to in front of the skyscraper and put into buses. Before you got onto the buses and when you were moving towards the centre, did you observe as to what has happened to the houses or what was happening around?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: The houses were burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: These houses, to whom did these belong to?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: They were Muslims'.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, before you got into the bus, did you see any other persons, people killed on the street?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the market in front of the kiosks, three or four people were lying there, burnt to the bone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of these persons who were around, who was dead or who was --

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see any Serb soldiers or any persons, any armed personnel there?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: There were lots of them around us, armed soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were put onto buses and taken to Omarska. Before you were taken to Omarska, were you taken to the SUP building, the bus that you were in?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: No. I wasn't, but it stopped there for a short time in front of the SUP building, and some people were taken out there. Some were returned, others I don't know. And then we went off towards Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see the people who returned to the bus as to what their physical condition was, and as to who took them from the buses and brought them back?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: The policemen took them out and the policemen brought them back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What was their physical -- the condition of the people who were taken from the buses?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Well, they were in a good state.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, after you left the SUP building, the bus that you were in, you said that the buses reached Omarska. Is it the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: The Omarska camp, yes. We went via Tomasica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When you reached Omarska, what were you ordered to do, and by whom?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: We were ordered to get out of the bus, to stand against the wall, lift our hands up. We were searched and then thrown into the room by the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, a room, you say. Is that a room which was in the administration building, the restaurant building?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The administration building, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you taken out of that room the next day to the pista?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: To the pista, yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you spend the night, the night that you arrived in the camp, in the room in the restaurant building?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Who were the others who was in that room in the restaurant building?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: They were the people from Prijedor who came that night and who were collected up in town during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know which ethnicity they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Non-Serb nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, the next day, you said that you were taken to the pista. When you were in the pista, were you able to see around?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Sometimes yes, sometimes no. Sometimes we had to look down onto the asphalt, and at other times we would have to lie down on our stomachs, our faces facing the asphalt.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Who gave these orders? Who made them, made you all do this?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: The guards made us do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you know a person by the name of Miroslav Kvocka?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know him before the war?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: I did, superficially.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know whom he was married to?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Please, do you know the name?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Jasminka, Jasminka Crnalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How did you know her?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: I knew her. She lives one house from mine, two houses away from mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now Witness, you said that you knew Miroslav Kvocka before. Did you know how he was employed?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Superficially, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How he was employed, where he was employed?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Kvocka worked in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was he a policeman?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How would you describe Miroslav Kvocka when you saw him before the war?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: He was tall, brown, slim.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Would you describe his hair?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Brown hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did you see Miroslav Kvocka when you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How was he dressed when you saw him in the camp?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: In a police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What else did you observe? Did he carry a weapon?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He had a pump-action gun and gloves on his hands with the fingers cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Where would you normally see him, and doing what?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: I would see him when we were at the pista, passing by. He kept going back and forth to the administration building. He was moving around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know what position he held or what authority he had in the camp?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know and what I heard from others, he was the commander of the camp for a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see him giving orders to any of the guards or any other personnel in the camp?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: During the day, he would issue orders, but I couldn't hear what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Issuing orders to whom?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: To the guards. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Krstan Simic. MR. K. SIMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness explicitly said that he couldn't hear what Mr. Kvocka was saying to the guards, and then came the question that he issued orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Krstan Simic, but the witness said that he couldn't hear, but he supposedly saw, and that is why the question followed. Therefore, the objection is overruled and you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: My question was, did you see as to whom he issued orders to?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: To the guards. Who else?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, while you were in the camp, detained in the camp, did you see a person by the name of Slavko Ecimovic?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know him prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What was the first time? When did you see Slavko Ecimovic in the camp?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: I saw Slavko for the first time in the camp when he was brought to the camp. He was brought to the camp, his hands were tied, and his legs were tied, and he had wire around his mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said that you saw him brought to the camp. Where did you see him --

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: -- brought?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: They brought him to the pista, and he passed in front of us, and they took him upstairs to the administration building. I was at the pista at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You said that his hands were tied and his legs were tied, and a wire around his mouth. Did you see what physical condition he was in?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Could you say how?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD HASKIC
